ideas.whySimpler: It removes the requirement that the client learn a new behaviour at all. Reply is the most natural action in an inbox and the current plan makes it a black hole. In the field, one reply that goes unanswered teaches a fleet operator that the system does not listen, and they stop responding through every channel — including the link you wanted them to use. Not parsing replies protects the system; ignoring replies punishes the client.
ideas.risks: I am arguing against an agreed decision, so its objections have to be answered rather than waved off: forged senders are handled by never trusting From and never auto-applying anything; auto-reply loops by the header filters plus a cap of one receipt per case per hour; quotes and signatures by not parsing and putting a human in front. Residual risks are real. Plus-addressing is disabled on some cPanel plans — verify on this host before designing around it. A tagged address that leaks attracts spam into an operational mailbox. The receipt itself can bounce or ping-pong against a badly behaved autoresponder. And client replies now sit in a shared mailbox that several Teletrac staff can read, which is a privacy fact worth telling GTL rather than discovering later.

ideas.title: Threads are born from conversation; routine detection lives in one collapsing digest
ideas.clientExperience: His inbox has one GTL row that never multiplies: "GTL fleet — July 2026", updated each morning, preview line "9 vehicles offline, 2 need your input". Inside, today's list with a tap-target beside the two that need him. He only ever gets a separate per-vehicle row when there is a genuine back-and-forth about that vehicle, and when it settles the final message says the case is closed and nothing more will arrive on it — so he can archive it without wondering.
ideas.mechanism: The digest subject is stable for a calendar month ("GTL fleet — July 2026") and each day's digest is sent In-Reply-To the month's root, so thirty emails occupy one inbox row and roll over before Gmail starts trimming. A per-vehicle thread is created only when (a) we ask the client a specific question, (b) the client says something about that vehicle, or (c) a case closes. Routine re-detection of an already-known-offline vehicle never sends mail; it just updates the digest. Unanswered questions nudge inside the existing thread on a decaying schedule — day 3, day 10 — never daily.
ideas.whySimpler: The client's real problem is not finding the emails, it is the volume. Forty offline vehicles must not become forty inbox rows on a phone. This makes the default state exactly one row, and makes any additional row carry a genuine meaning: this specific vehicle needs you. It also matters for data cost — one digest a day is a fraction of the bytes of forty threads.
ideas.risks: A stable digest subject means a client who mutes or filters it mutes everything at once, so per-vehicle threads must never inherit that subject line. Monthly rollover is one deliberate thread break a year times twelve — accept it, or the thread eventually becomes unusable. If GTL forwards the digest internally, only the digest travels and none of the per-vehicle context goes with it. The volume discipline is a policy, not code: the first time a technician CCs the client on an internal action the whole benefit starts eroding, so enforce it in the send path rather than in a wiki. And underneath all of this, low volume from a shared cPanel IP still needs SPF, DKIM and DMARC to be correct — if GTL's Gmail bins these into spam, every idea above is moot and nobody will find out for weeks.

verdicts.fatalFlaw: Two survive scrutiny, neither quite kills it. (1) As specified, the mechanism does not actually thread. A frozen subject plus Thread-Topic is not sufficient for Gmail — Gmail groups on References/In-Reply-To first and only falls back to subject heuristics, and these are messages the client never replied to, so there is no chain at all. Apple Mail threads purely on References. Shipping this as written gets you a pile of identical-subject messages that are HARDER to tell apart than today's descriptive ones, i.e. the exact failure mode inverted. The idea's own risk list never mentions Message-ID, In-Reply-To or References, which suggests the author reasoned about rendering and not about grouping. (2) Even done correctly, any recipient whose client has conversation view off (classic Outlook desktop, some POP/IMAP setups) sees an undifferentiated wall of "[GTL] KDN480R - Toyota Hiace HR55 123A" rows, distinguishable only by timestamp, and if Message Preview is also off there is literally zero information in the list. For that population this is a strict regression. Both are fixable; neither is a reason to reject, but (1) means the idea as literally written would fail in production.
verdicts.requiredChanges:
1. ADD THE THREADING HEADERS — this is the actual mechanism, not an optional extra. Mint a deterministic per-vehicle root: Message-ID `<gtl-KDN480R@teletracfleets.com>` on the FIRST email for that plate; every later email gets its own unique Message-ID plus `In-Reply-To: <gtl-KDN480R@...>` and `References: <gtl-KDN480R@...>`. Deterministic from the plate means nothing has to be stored, nothing can race, and nothing forks. Cap References at root + last 2 ids so the header does not grow unbounded.

2. DROP THE VEHICLE DESCRIPTION FROM THE SUBJECT. Use `[GTL] KDN480R` only. The idea's own last risk note admits the description string must be persisted or a fleet re-import silently forks every thread — that is a self-inflicted wound. On Render free tier with ephemeral disk and Google Sheets as the only store, a value that must survive forever and be byte-identical is a liability: you buy a Sheets read+write on every send, a Sheets quota exposure on burst sends, and a read-modify-write race between the cron sender and the feedback-triggered sender that permanently forks a thread when it loses. Make subject a pure function of the plate (the one immutable key, already the sheet's primary key in `sheets_store.py`) and the entire storage layer, cache layer and race disappear. Make/model belongs on body line 2 where it is more readable anyway. This change alone moves effort from medium to small.

3. NO NEW SHEETS TAB. With 1 and 2 there is nothing to persist. If anyone proposes a Threads tab keyed by plate, that is the signal the design drifted back to stored state.

4. BUDGET ~45 CHARS FOR THE SNIPPET, NOT 90. Gmail Android on a narrow phone truncates well short of 80. "No follow-up needed - Known Issues" (34) works; "Feedback received from you. No follow-up needed - moved to Known Issues." does not — it truncates before the verdict on some devices. Write every status line verdict-first and test at 45.

5. HARD RULE IN THE TEMPLATE: the status line is the first rendered node in the body. No logo table, no "view in browser", no preheader. Add a test that asserts the first 60 chars of stripped body text equal the status line — otherwise the first person to add branding silently destroys the entire benefit, and nobody will notice because the emails still look fine when opened.

6. MAKE EACH MESSAGE SELF-CONTAINED FOR FORWARDING. The thread history lives only in Glenn's mailbox; a forward to a colleague or an insurer carries one message. Include the last 3 trail entries inline below the status line. Cheap, and it also covers the shared-mailbox case where a colleague opened it first.

7. FALLBACK FLAG PER RECIPIENT. One boolean, `descriptive_subjects`, defaulting off. If anyone reports the wall-of-identical-lines problem (conversation view off), flip it for that address and append the event to the subject for them. Costs a config field and removes the only population this genuinely harms. Verify the actual client mix before rollout rather than assuming Gmail.

8. NOTIFY ON STATE CHANGE ONLY, NOT DAILY. This defends the Gmail ~100-message conversation split without needing the separate mechanism the idea defers to "idea 3", and it independently reduces client load.

NON-ISSUES I CHECKED AND CLEARED: patchy mobile data is fine (the point is that no click is needed to get the status); Render cold start is irrelevant since sending is server-initiated and correctness does not depend on latency; email-scanner prefetch is a property of the feedback token URL, not of this idea, provided that page stays GET-idempotent and the token is not consumed on view; shared-mailbox unread state is unchanged since a new message re-bolds the conversation. One honest cost that cannot be engineered away: threads sort by recency, so the inbox becomes a recency list rather than a severity list — a vehicle offline 30 days sinks below one that just resolved. Accept it; the status line carries the severity.

verdicts.fatalFlaw: Not fatal, but the strongest argument against: false-closure emails. Closure keyed on "clear for N days" is evaluated on a Render free-tier stack where the daily import may simply not run (Apps Script miss, cold-start timeout, import failure) — and absence of data is indistinguishable from absence of problem. The system then emails Glenn "KDN480R is resolved, this thread is closed" about a truck that is still offline. One such email poisons every future email from the system, and it is exactly the failure a fleet operator will remember. Secondary: the headline justification is wrong. The Gmail ~100-message hard split is real but irrelevant at this system's volume (roughly 3-15 messages per vehicle per year — Glenn reaches 100 in a decade), so "Gmail splits it anyway, better we control it" is a rationalization. The idea survives only because a completely different argument holds independently: an open thread means an open problem, archiving is a real end state, and an immortal thread can never be archived so it sits in the inbox forever and the inbox stops meaning anything. Judge and defend the idea on that basis, not the 100-message one.
verdicts.requiredChanges:
1. CLOSURE MUST REQUIRE POSITIVE EVIDENCE, NOT ELAPSED TIME. Close only after N *successful imports* in which the asset was observed and found clear. Store observation count and last-observed-date on the ledger row. A day with no import, a failed import, or an asset missing from the feed advances nothing. Silent non-closure (thread stays open) is the safe failure; premature closure is not.

2. TWO DISTINCT TERMINAL STATES, DIFFERENT WORDING. "Resolved" (asset observed clear) and "Parked" (client set requiresFollowup=false, lands in Known Issues per sheets_store.infer_status). Known Issue means stop chasing, NOT fixed. A parked case must close with wording like "we're no longer chasing this; tell us if that changes" — never resolution language.

3. A PARKED CASE MUST NOT REOPEN ON THE SAME CONDITION. The 14-day reopen window is insufficient: a Known Issue asset stays flagged indefinitely and will mint case 5, 6, 7 forever. The ledger must record a suppression keyed to the condition that was parked, lifted only when the condition materially changes or the client says otherwise. Without this, requiresFollowup=false becomes a case-generation engine.

4. HARD CAP: ONE OPEN CASE PER VEHICLE, ALWAYS. A new symptom on an asset with an open case joins that case. Never two live threads for one plate.

5. DROP "(case 4)" AS THE SUBJECT DIFFERENTIATOR — USE THE CASE'S START DATE. "case 4" is internal jargon to a fleet operator. Use "[GTL] KDN480R Toyota Hiace - offline since 14 Mar". This is equally effective against Gmail's subject-similarity re-merge, is meaningful to Glenn, and it is the actual resolution of the descriptive-vs-stable tension: the subject describes the CASE (stable for the case's whole life), while per-event description moves to the first line of the body, which Gmail renders as the thread-list snippet. Descriptive and stable at the same time. State this explicitly as the threading rule.

6. THE CLOSING MESSAGE MUST CARRY A TOKENISED "THIS ISN'T FIXED" BUTTON. Case closure sharply raises the odds Glenn replies to a dead thread to object, and inbound replies are deliberately not parsed. His affordance for disagreeing must be a button to a reopen page, not a reply. Because email scanners prefetch links, the GET must only render the page; reopening must require a POST from that page.

7. IDEMPOTENT SEND ORDERING. Send the closing email first, then mark the ledger row closed, guarded by a closingSent flag — a free-tier process killed mid-cron must re-send, never skip. A thread that dies without its closing message is worse than no case scoping at all.

8. NEW MUTABLE SHEETS TAB, EXPLICITLY OUT-OF-BAND FROM THE APPEND-ONLY FEEDBACK TRAIL. sheets_store.py is append-only by design; do not bend it. Add an "Incidents" tab (plate, caseNo, threadGuid, rootMessageId, subjectLine, openedAt, lastEventAt, observedClearCount, state, closedAt, closingSent, suppressUntil). Correctness must never depend on the ephemeral _feedback_stamp file — cold starts must read the ledger from Sheets.

9. GET THE USER'S EXPLICIT SIGN-OFF ON REFUSING THE STATED REQUIREMENT. This deliberately does not deliver "all emails about one vehicle in one thread." It delivers the underlying intent (no pile of scattered messages) while preserving search-by-plate. That trade is defensible but it is the user's call, not ours.

verdicts.fatalFlaw: The follow-up decision is encoded in an opaque recipient address (reply+KDN480R.c1.no.a7f3c9e2b1@...), so the client can neither see nor correct what they committed to before sending. If Glenn taps "No follow-up needed" and then types "actually the device is gone, send a tech," the address wins and the asset silently drops out of the Critical Assets queue — a state change app.py:284 currently forces to be an explicit, visible choice. The only fix is to put intent in the body, which reintroduces the inbound parsing the design deliberately avoided. Compounding this, the idea's central justification ("cold-started Render page is the worst step") is removable for about ten lines: apps_script_scheduler.gs currently installs only a DAILY 4:15 AM trigger, and adding an everyMinutes(10) keep-warm ping — which the reply-reader would need anyway — makes the tokenised page a normal 1-3s load. So it pays for a second full ingestion channel to buy something the cheap fix already delivers.
verdicts.requiredChanges:
Do not ship as proposed. Ship the cheap substitutes that capture most of the value:

1. Add an everyMinutes(10) keep-warm trigger to apps_script_scheduler.gs (which today installs only a daily 4:15 AM trigger). This removes the cold-start penalty that motivated the whole idea and is a prerequisite for any inbound-reply polling anyway.

2. Steal the one genuinely good sub-idea: make the comment OPTIONAL on the tokenised web page for the "No follow-up needed" path, so it is tap-link, tap-button, done. This is the actual client-effort reduction, and it works on every mail client, unlike mailto: body prefill.

3. Solve single-thread-per-vehicle separately and properly: stable subject "[GTL] KDN480R - Toyota Hiace" on every message, plus a synthetic per-vehicle root Message-ID (e.g. <gtl.KDN480R@teletracfleets.com>) that every subsequent outbound message carries in References/In-Reply-To. Put the changing event description in the preheader and first line of the body, never in the subject. mailto: does not help here — it composes a new message with no In-Reply-To to a different recipient than the original sender, which weakens Gmail's participant+subject fallback rather than strengthening it.

Only revisit mailto: if, after (1) and (2), real usage shows clients actually failing to complete the web flow on connectivity grounds. If revisited, it must be: (a) intent NOT encoded in the address — a single neutral reply address per vehicle, with follow-up state left unchanged and defaulted to requiresFollowup=true, technician-confirmed; (b) presented as one fallback link in small text, never as co-equal buttons; (c) dedup via IMAP \Seen plus Message-ID recorded in Sheets, since Render's ephemeral disk gives no durable seen-store; (d) a strict folder allowlist so the reply reader can never touch the report folders importer/mail_reader.py depends on; (e) an immediate outcome email confirming exactly what was recorded, so the client is never left in silence.

verdicts.fatalFlaw: It optimises inside the wrong unit, and the numbers say so. `data/fleet_today.json` has 126 assets with 16 escalations + 7 pending + 6 double-flagged — roughly 20-25 "problem" vehicles on a normal day. "At most one email per truck per day" therefore lands ~20 emails a day in Glenn's inbox, forever, about largely the SAME long-term faults (the severity band is literally "Critical - Long-term Fault"). The idea's headline claim — "the inbox stops being a firehose... the number of unread items IS the number of things to deal with" — is false at this fleet's actual scale; 20/day IS the firehose. The per-vehicle ceiling only looks like a reduction if you assume six events per truck per day, and the system cannot produce that: telemetry refreshes once daily via the 4:15 AM import, so there is at most one system-generated event per vehicle per day ALREADY. The coalescing machinery is built to suppress a burst the architecture cannot emit. The genuinely simpler thing for Glenn — one daily digest per CLIENT, 20 rows, each with its own tokenised link — is never considered, because the idea inherited the per-vehicle-thread constraint and optimised inside it instead of questioning it. Secondary flaw, self-contradiction: the premise is "threading is genuinely absent for a large share of recipients," but the history-hiding mechanism (Gmail's "..." trimmer collapsing content that matches the previous message in the thread) only fires when threading IS present. In the forwarded copy and conversation-view-off cases the idea is designed for, the quote block renders fully expanded. And since the 3-entry cap already means "must look fine fully expanded," the gmail_quote trick buys nothing and costs template fragility. Not disqualifying overall, because the self-sufficiency half survives all of this independently.
verdicts.requiredChanges:
ADOPT (unchanged): the self-sufficiency principle. Plate, fault, current status, and both buttons above the fold, comprehensible with zero prior messages. This is the single best idea in the set — it survives forwarding, shared mailboxes, conversation-view-off, and patchy data (a synced email needs no network; the whole point is Glenn never loads a page). Keep it.

DROP: the `gmail_quote`/`blockquote type="cite"` collapse trick. Render the last 3 trail entries as plain small text under a divider. Same visual outcome in the case that matters, no dependency on an undocumented heuristic, no client-specific CSS. (`<details>` is not a substitute — Gmail won't toggle it.)

DROP: the batch runner, the per-vehicle event queue tab, and the severity bypass. On this dataset there is nothing to coalesce, and the bypass is pure surface area — a bypass that fires means two emails that day, which breaks the one promise the idea makes. Replace all of it with one rule: a `lastNotifiedDate` column per plate in the Sheet; suppress a system notification if one already went today. Ten lines, no new cron, no new failure mode.

DROP: the warm-up ping, and note the reasoning is backwards. A `UrlFetchApp` timeout does not cancel the server-side request — Render keeps processing it. So the failure mode is not "the batch silently does not send"; it is Apps Script seeing a timeout, the operator or a retry re-firing, and the client getting DUPLICATE emails. Duplicates are strictly worse than a delayed send. Fix with an idempotency ledger in Sheets keyed on (plate, date, eventHash), checked before send, not with a second cron. Better still: emit sends from inside the existing `/api/import` request, which is already warm.

ADD (this is the actual answer to the question that was asked, and the idea ducks it): stable subject, descriptive preheader. Subject is frozen forever per vehicle — `[GTL] KDN480R - Fleet Integrity` — and never varies by event. The event description ("feedback received, no follow-up needed") moves into the hidden preheader span, which Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail all render as the grey preview line next to the subject in the list view. Glenn gets a descriptive list line AND an unbroken thread. That is the resolution of the stated tension; declaring threading optional is a hedge, not an answer, and the hedge is worth having alongside a real implementation, not instead of one.

ADD: persist the first `Message-ID` per plate in the Sheet (Render's disk is ephemeral — `sheets_store.py` is the only store) and set `In-Reply-To`/`References` on every subsequent send. Without this, threading cannot work at all across restarts.

ADD: define "event" as a state TRANSITION only — newly offline, severity change, tamper confirmed, feedback received, technician action. "Still offline, day 47" is never an event. Without this the daily ceiling silently becomes a daily heartbeat and the ~20/day becomes ~600/month about 16 unchanged trucks. Note `recovered: 0` and `newlyOffline: 0` in the current snapshot: transitions are rare, which is what makes the batch runner disproportionate and this rule cheap.

FIX (concrete bug the idea walks into): do not hotlink `static/Teletrac_Fleet_Solutions_logo.png` from the Render instance. A sleeping free-tier instance means a 30-60s hang then a broken image in every email, on exactly the patchy mobile data the idea claims to survive. Inline it as CID or drop it.

KEEP: feedback receipts send immediately, and the run outcome logs to the Sheet and surfaces to technicians only, never the client. Both correct.

verdicts.fatalFlaw: The novel part — the client's personal name in the From display name — is precisely the display-name-mismatch signature that Microsoft Defender's mailbox-intelligence user-impersonation protection is built to catch: an external, low-reputation sender (a cPanel-hosted mail.teletracfleets.com, none of GitHub's or Google Groups' allow-listing or IP reputation) carrying the display name of a person the recipient's mailbox has learned arrives from a different domain. The result is a "this message seems dangerous / be careful" banner on the exact message engineered to be the trustworthy receipt, which attacks client simplicity harder than anything it fixes. Not fatal to the underlying idea, because the receipt-lands-in-the-same-thread mechanism survives intact without the name in the header. Two further arguments the proposal never considered: (1) humanising the sender invites Reply-All, and replies live only in email — since the team explicitly does not parse inbound mail, every reply silently diverges the "thread is the record" from the Sheet, so the pitch quietly becomes false the first time anyone hits reply; (2) a forwarded email leaks the tokenised link, and under this design whoever uses it produces a message that asserts Glenn's identity in his colleagues' inboxes — the idea amplifies a pre-existing token weakness into an attribution-forgery hole. Also note the receipt's "did it register?" value is partly redundant with the confirmation page — except, and this is what saves it, on 3G plus a 30-60s Render cold start the POST often succeeds while the response never reaches the phone, so the emailed receipt is the only proof that survives the environment they actually operate in.
verdicts.requiredChanges:
1. DROP the client's personal name from the From header. Send `From: "GTL Control Room" <control-room@teletracfleets.com>` — constant, boring, reputation-building. Move attribution to three safer channels that carry it just as well: the preheader/snippet (first ~90 chars of body, which is what Gmail renders next to the stable subject in a phone list view), a bold attribution line at the top of the body ("Glenn Kato, GTL — 27 Jul 14:10"), and, if you want the who-touched-this signal in the inbox list, add the acting person as a Cc'd or From-adjacent participant rather than as a spoofed display name. If you keep any name in the display slot, restrict it to the Teletrac side ("Control Room — technician update"), never a name the recipient's own directory knows.

2. THIS IS THE ACTUAL SUBJECT-TENSION RESOLUTION, so make it explicit: subject is frozen forever per vehicle (`[GTL] KDN480R — device offline`), and the entire variable "what happened this time" payload goes in the preheader. That is the channel that is per-message, visible in list view without opening, and costs nothing. The display-name trick was a weaker substitute for it.

3. KILL THE SEQ COUNTER. The proposal's "new Message-ID (seq+1)" is unnecessary and unsafe here. Threading only requires that `References` (and `In-Reply-To`) contain a known ancestor ID; the message's own Message-ID can be fully random. So: root ID is deterministic from the plate alone — `<gtl-KDN480R@teletracfleets.com>` — needing zero new state, which matters because Render's disk is ephemeral and the Sheet is the only store. Every subsequent message sets `References: <gtl-KDN480R@teletracfleets.com>` and its own random Message-ID. This removes the duplicate-ID silent-drop failure the proposal correctly feared, removes any read-then-write race between the Apps Script cron and a live request, and removes the need for a Message-ID column in the Feedback tab. Worth noting concretely: `sheets_store.py:30` defines `FEEDBACK_HEADERS` and lines 107-108 rewrite row 1 whenever it does not match, so adding a column is a live schema migration with blank historic rows — avoid it. Also note `DateAdded` is written at minute resolution with no timezone (`sheets_store.py:345`), so timestamps in the sheet cannot serve as a unique sequence either.

4. Do NOT strip non-ASCII from header text. Use RFC 2047 encoded-words via Python's `email.headerregistry` / `Header`, which encodes UTF-8 safely and eliminates CR/LF by construction. Stripping non-ASCII mangles East African names in the one artifact whose whole job is to look trustworthy. Keep the CR/LF defence; implement it as "let the stdlib build the header", not as a regex.

5. Send per-recipient (individual sends or Bcc), not one message with everyone in To/Cc. This is needed anyway because the "Give Feedback" link must be a per-person token, and it simultaneously defuses the Reply-All branch. Identical `References` on each copy still threads correctly in every client.

6. Bind the token to one recipient address and make the recorded attribution honest — "submitted via the link sent to glenn@…" — rather than an asserted identity. This is what makes forwarding harmless instead of forgeable.

7. Set an expectation about replies, since Reply-To points at the technician group: one line, "Replies reach the team but do not update the vehicle record — use the button to add to the record." Without it, "the thread is the record" is a promise the system breaks silently.

8. Keep `Auto-Submitted: auto-generated` (correct, and correct that it beats `Precedence: bulk`). Keep the "your comment is shared with the Teletrac team" note on the feedback page.

9. Hard boundary: this receipt must only ever be emitted from a POST. Never wire the follow-up yes/no to a one-click GET link in the email — an email-scanner prefetch would set requiresFollowup=false, pull the asset out of the Critical Assets queue, and then broadcast a message claiming the client said no follow-up was needed.

verdicts.fatalFlaw: The durable thread ledger is unnecessary state that buys nothing the client can see, and its named concurrency primitive is broken. `_claim_refresh_lock` (app.py:396) is a rate limiter, not a mutex: it never releases on success and only clears via stale-steal after LOCK_COOLDOWN_MINUTES=10, so the second gunicorn worker gets False, has no seq, no wait and no retry, and the alert email is simply never sent for up to ten minutes. Its lock file also sits on the same ephemeral disk the idea correctly argues state cannot live on. Meanwhile the outcome needs no ledger at all: pointing every message's In-Reply-To/References at a derived phantom root gives identical client-visible threading in Gmail, Apple Mail, Thunderbird and Outlook with zero writes, zero Sheets quota, zero locks, and no 1-4s round-trip added to the send path behind a cold start. Secondary but serious: unbounded per-vehicle threading is a client-simplicity regression, because Gmail's Mute is per-thread and permanent, so one mute silently auto-archives every future alert for that vehicle including the critical one three months later, and neither side finds out.
verdicts.requiredChanges:
1) DROP the Threads tab, Seq, RootMessageId, LastMessageId and the atomic claim entirely. Derive the root instead: every message carries In-Reply-To and References of `<gtl.{PLATE}.{EPISODE}@teletracfleets.com>`, a phantom root that is never sent. JWZ clients build a dummy container for the absent root; Gmail groups on shared References plus matching normalised subject. This removes the Sheets 60-writes/min throttle risk, the batching complication, the redeploy-loses-the-row recovery path, and all send-path I/O.

2) DO NOT reuse `_claim_refresh_lock` for anything requiring uniqueness. Randomise each message's own Message-ID (uuid4). This is required regardless: one deterministic Message-ID sent to all recipients collides with per-recipient tokenised feedback links, since Gmail dedupes on Message-ID and a shared client inbox would lose one contact's token. Randomised IDs also make the SMTP-retry question moot.

3) KEY ON EPISODE, NOT VEHICLE-FOREVER. Promote the case number from disaster recovery to the primary thread key: one thread per offline episode, keyed on the date the vehicle went offline. Bounds mute/filter blast radius to one incident, keeps threads short, keeps the frozen subject truthful. A Gmail search on the plate still gathers every episode.

4) RESOLVE THE SUBJECT TENSION EXPLICITLY (the idea names FrozenSubject and never defines it). Freeze the subject to `[KDN480R] Offline since 12 Jul` and never append to it — Gmail normalises only Re:/Fwd: prefixes, any suffix forks. Carry the per-event description in the PREHEADER, the first ~90 chars of body text, which Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail all render inline after the subject in list view. Inbox line becomes `[KDN480R] Offline since 12 Jul — Feedback received: no follow-up needed`. Repeat it as the body's first line for clients that don't show preheaders.

5) DEFER Thread-Index behind a verification step. The 22-byte construction described is correct (0x01 + 5 FILETIME bytes + 16 GUID bytes, base64 to 32 chars) and the 5-byte child block can be time-derived with no stored state, but modern Outlook and Exchange already honour References for inbound internet mail. Confirm GTL actually reads mail in Outlook classic before building it; ship References-only first.

6) ADD `Auto-Submitted: auto-generated` and `X-Auto-Response-Suppress: All` — these, not the List-Unsubscribe reasoning, are what prevent the vacation-responder loops this design exists to avoid. Keep List-Id for filtering but drop the stated justification for omitting List-Unsubscribe; it is folk wisdom and inconsistent (List-Id is at least as strong a bulk signal). Omitting it is fine at this volume, just not for that reason.

SCOPE NOTE: no outbound mail exists in the codebase today — importer/mail_reader.py is IMAP read-only and requirements.txt has no mail sender. The threading layer amended as above is small (a header-builder function plus an episode key). The greenfield SMTP send path, templates and recipient config underneath it are the bulk of the work and should be scoped separately.

threading.rec: Resolve it by refusing the premise that the subject line is where description belongs. The tension only exists if you assume the client reads the subject to learn what happened — on a phone, they don't. Gmail, Apple Mail and Outlook mobile all render the inbox row as **sender + subject + one line of snippet**, and the snippet is drawn from the preheader, which is per-message and completely irrelevant to threading. So: the subject carries **identity only** — `UAX 123J`, byte-identical forever, generated by a single function that takes no formatting arguments. The preheader carries the **event** — `Feedback received — no follow-up needed`, `Now offline 14 days, escalated`, `Technician dispatched`. The client loses nothing; in fact the description gets *more* room in the snippet (~90 chars) than a truncated mobile subject line gives it (~35 chars). You end up with strictly more visible information and clean threading, not a trade-off. Back it with a **deterministic root Message-ID derived from the plate** (`<gtl.veh.UAX123J.root@teletracfleets.com>`) plus a `Threads` tab in the existing spreadsheet holding the last Message-ID and References chain — deterministic because Render's ephemeral disk means any state store can vanish, and a recomputable root means total state loss degrades to \"one message lacks In-Reply-To\" rather than \"the thread forks permanently\". The operational rule that matters more than any header: nothing may ever be appended to that subject. Not a status, not a date, not a count, not a `Re:`. One vehicle, one row in the inbox, for the life of the asset.

Do not try to make one subject line do two jobs — it cannot, and every clever attempt (counters, appended status, bracketed tags) fragments the thread in Gmail and Outlook anyway, because Gmail requires a matching normalised subject on top of References, and Outlook derives ConversationTopic from the subject. Resolve it by moving the per-event description to a different surface that is BETTER at the job.

Concretely: (1) The subject is minted once per INCIDENT and is thereafter immutable, byte for byte — "KDN480R · Offline since 12 Jul · GTL-1183". No "Re:" prefix (both Gmail and Outlook normalise it away, and omitting it avoids "Re: Re:" in clients that don't). (2) The per-event headline lives in a hidden preheader div at the top of the body, which is what Gmail actually renders as the inbox snippet — it gets ~100 characters, more room than a subject line, updates on every message, and has no prefix-safety constraints. The client's inbox row therefore reads descriptively and changes per event while the subject never moves. Pad the preheader with repeated ‌  so real body copy cannot bleed into the snippet. (3) Send In-Reply-To = previous Message-ID and References = the full accumulated chain, stored in the Google Sheet keyed on Plate + IncidentId, never on Render's ephemeral disk. (4) Break the thread deliberately in exactly one place and nowhere else: when an incident closes, the next problem on that vehicle opens a new incident number and a new root. One thread per vehicle forever is not simpler for the client, it is a tomb — a 400-message conversation spanning three years is worse than the pile it replaced. One thread per live problem matches how the client already thinks. (5) Belt and braces: set From and Reply-To to kdn480r@fleet.teletracfleets.com so that even if some client fragments the thread, "from:kdn480r" recovers the entire history in one search, and a filter is trivial to build.

The deeper recommendation: ration threads by decisions owed, not by events emitted. Routine status belongs in one standing digest thread; a vehicle earns its own thread only when it crosses into Critical or High. And accept that the highest-leverage simplification is not threading at all — it is removing the 30-60 second Render cold start from the client's critical path, via mailto: one-click replies or a WhatsApp button, so the common case ("this is a known issue, leave it alone") never requires a page load on patchy mobile data.

Resolve it by moving the description, not by weakening the threading — and by accepting that the subject line was never where the client was reading anyway.

Concretely: the subject encodes identity and only identity, byte-stable for the life of the vehicle (`[KDN 480R] Vehicle status — Teletrac`). No verbs, no status, no dates, no 'Re:' games. Every descriptive word goes into the preheader — the hidden block at the top of the body that Gmail and Outlook mobile render right beside the subject in the message list. That is the same visual slot a descriptive subject would have occupied, at roughly the same character budget, read in the same glance. The client loses nothing they were actually getting. Thread continuity comes from a phantom `References:` root derived as `hmac(THREAD_SECRET, plate)[:12]`, which is stateless (survives Render's ephemeral disk and every redeploy with no storage), deterministic (regenerates identically forever), and unguessable — that last property matters specifically *because* the subject is now predictable: a stable subject plus a guessable Message-ID is an open invitation to inject a phishing message into the client's own trusted thread.

Two things must not follow from 'one thread per vehicle'. First, one thread does not mean one message to everyone. The outcome email as currently specced goes to client contacts + technicians + admins, and if that is one send with one body it routes around `permissions.py` entirely — `reasons` and `borderDetail` and tamper context landing in a client inbox that the dashboard is careful to withhold them from. Send two messages with two bodies under two different phantom roots. They are separate threads that happen to be about the same truck.

Second, a stable thread trains people to hit Reply. This is where I disagree with the agreed direction. Not parsing inbound replies into *state* is correct, and I'd keep it — forged senders, quote stripping, and auto-reply loops are all real, and nothing that arrives by unauthenticated email should ever be able to move a vehicle out of the critical queue. But a reply that silently vanishes is a worse client experience than not threading at all: Glenn believes he has been heard, and he hasn't. Set `Reply-To:` to a genuinely monitored technician address, say so in the footer ('Reply to this email and a technician will read it'), and if you want it in the trail, ingest replies as unverified text only — appended to the history, clearly badged, never touching `requiresFollowup`. The security property that matters is preserved: only a token-bound POST or an authenticated dashboard session can change operational state. And to stop the thread poisoning itself, every outbound message needs `Auto-Submitted: auto-generated`, `X-Auto-Response-Suppress: All`, `Precedence: bulk`, and a dedicated bounce Return-Path — otherwise one out-of-office from one recipient on a five-person distribution list starts a loop inside the client's tidy new thread.

Resolve it by demoting the subject from headline to name. The subject line is the thread's IDENTIFIER, not its content — freeze it byte-for-byte per vehicle-case (`[GTL] KDN480R - Toyota Hiace HR55 123A`, pure ASCII, no dates, no status, no emoji) and never touch it again. The descriptive part moves to the first visible line of the body, because Gmail web, Gmail mobile, Outlook mobile and Apple Mail all render that as the snippet directly beside the subject in the list view, and for a multi-message thread Gmail shows the snippet of the NEWEST message. So the client gets a changing, descriptive line in their inbox AND an unbroken thread — the two goals were only in conflict because both were being loaded onto the same header. This is not a compromise; it is what GitHub (`[org/repo] Title (#123)`), Linear (`[TEAM-123] Title`) and Intercom all do. Concretely: Gmail and Superhuman require BOTH a resolving References/In-Reply-To chain AND a matching normalized subject (it strips Re:/Fwd:/Aw:/SV: but not `[GTL]`), so the frozen subject is non-negotiable there; Apple Mail and Thunderbird thread on References alone; Outlook classic/web/mobile use Exchange ConversationId, seeded from a synthesised 22-byte `Thread-Index` when present, else from a hash of normalized `Thread-Topic` — so emit both a stable-GUID Thread-Index and a Thread-Topic equal to the frozen subject. `List-Id` helps filtering and Superhuman split-inbox but threads nothing; skip `List-Unsubscribe` (pushes Gmail toward the Updates tab) and use `Auto-Submitted: auto-generated` rather than `Precedence: bulk`. The one place I would push back on the brief: \"one thread per vehicle forever\" is not actually achievable — Gmail force-splits conversations around 100 messages at a point we cannot choose or label — so scope threads to one incident/case with the plate as a permanent prefix, and control the split ourselves.

Resolve it by noticing that a phone inbox already shows two lines, and only one of them has to be stable. The Subject carries IDENTITY and never events: freeze it at case creation as plate plus case number — "KDN480R — GTL case 7" — short enough that the plate survives truncation on a small Android screen. Store that string, the root Message-ID and the References chain in the Google Sheet, because Render's disk is ephemeral and the Sheet is the only place a thread's identity can outlive a restart. Every subsequent message ships In-Reply-To: <root> plus the accumulated References. Everything descriptive — "feedback received: no follow-up needed" — moves to the three levers that can change freely without fragmenting anything: the preheader (the grey line under the subject, which is where a busy operator actually reads status and which most designs waste on "View this email in your browser"), the From display name, and the first visible line of the body, repeated verbatim for clients that render no preheader. That gives you a descriptive inbox row AND a single thread, with no conflict left. Two deliberate deviations from the literal ask. First, do not thread per vehicle forever: when a closed vehicle breaks again months later, increment the case number, which forks a new thread on purpose — threads that end can be archived, and a two-year thread hits Gmail's "show trimmed content" and becomes worse than useless. Second, do not open a per-vehicle thread on detection at all; open it only when a conversation genuinely starts. Routine offline detection belongs in one month-stable digest thread, so a client with forty offline vehicles sees one inbox row rather than forty. And none of this survives contact with reality unless the client-facing link opens fast — a perfectly threaded email whose button leads to 45 seconds of white screen on a cold Render dyno teaches the client to stop pressing it.
